fixes.explanation: Yes. The text says, “Nevertheless, the people refused to listen to Samuel.” Then they say, “No!” and “We must have a king over us.” (1 Samuel 8:19) Samuel just read out the full warning. They heard it and still said no.

The text never says they stopped holding court. Joel and Abijah were judges in Beersheba (1 Samuel 8:2). The text says they accepted bribes and perverted justice (1 Samuel 8:3). That's the trouble it names.

Nothing in this passage says that. The Philistines, whom Israel went out to meet in battle (1 Samuel 4:1), don't come up here. The text says the sons took bribes and perverted justice (1 Samuel 8:3). That's a problem right inside the courtroom.

Nobody's asking for a new priest, friend. The elders say, “Now appoint a king to judge us like all the other nations.” (1 Samuel 8:5) That's a job posting for a king, and a priest isn't anywhere in it.
That's right. The demand displeased Samuel, “so he prayed to the LORD.” (1 Samuel 8:6) The text says nothing about him storming out. When something stings, taking it to the LORD first is a good move.

Moses, who led Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10), isn't in this verse. The LORD tells Samuel, “…it is not you they have rejected, but they have rejected Me as their king.” (1 Samuel 8:7) He names Himself. So the answer sits with the LORD.

That's right. Samuel says, “And he will take your daughters to be perfumers, cooks, and bakers.” (1 Samuel 8:13) Bakers made the list, and I felt that one personally. Samuel says “he will take,” so it's the king doing the taking.
Weavers, potters and shepherds aren't on the list. Samuel says the king “…will take your daughters to be perfumers, cooks, and bakers.” (1 Samuel 8:13) That's three jobs, and it's a short list.

Yes. The people say they want “…a king to judge us, to go out before us, and to fight our battles.” (1 Samuel 8:20) That's the king they picture, going out before them and fighting. Samuel has just told them what that king will take.
